title: Hypertensive emergency and severe asymptomatic hypertension
subject: cardiology
summary: Hypertensive emergency is severe hypertension with acute organ damage: admit, use titratable IV drugs and lower BP to condition-specific targets (usually MAP down 20 to 25% over hours; immediately in aortic dissection, pulmonary oedema and ACS). Severe hypertension without organ damage is treated orally and gradually.

sections.title: Recognise: emergency or not
items: Hypertensive emergency: severe BP elevation (often 180/110 mmHg or more) with acute hypertension-mediated organ damage. The absolute BP is less important than the rate of rise and the organ damage.

Organ damage to look for: encephalopathy (headache, confusion, seizures, visual loss), stroke, acute coronary syndrome, acute pulmonary oedema, aortic dissection, acute kidney injury, eclampsia or severe pre-eclampsia.
Malignant hypertension: severe BP with retinal flame haemorrhages, cotton wool spots or papilloedema, often with thrombotic microangiopathy and AKI. Always perform fundoscopy.
Severe hypertension without acute organ damage (hypertensive urgency) is not an emergency: common causes are non-adherence, pain, anxiety and withdrawal; it does not need IV drugs or rapid lowering.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Fundoscopy, ECG, troponin, creatinine, electrolytes, urine dipstick (protein, blood) and microscopy.
CBC with blood film for schistocytes, LDH, haptoglobin and platelets (thrombotic microangiopathy).
Targeted imaging: CT or MRI brain for neurological signs; CT aortogram for suspected dissection; chest X-ray and echocardiography for pulmonary oedema.

Pregnancy test in women of reproductive age; urine drug screen where sympathomimetic use (cocaine, amphetamines) is suspected. Consider phaeochromocytoma, renal artery stenosis and primary aldosteronism once stable.

sections.title: General approach in an emergency
items: Admit to HDU or ICU with continuous BP monitoring (arterial line where possible) and use short-acting titratable IV drugs.

Unless a specific condition below applies, reduce MAP by no more than 20 to 25% over the first several hours, then towards 160/100 mmHg over the next 2 to 6 hours, then cautiously to normal over 24 to 48 hours.
Over-rapid lowering can cause cerebral, coronary or renal ischaemia, because autoregulation is shifted to higher pressures in chronic hypertension.
Do not give sublingual or immediate-release oral nifedipine or IV bolus hydralazine for non-pregnant adults: the fall in BP is unpredictable.
Patients are often volume depleted from pressure natriuresis; avoid routine diuretics unless there is pulmonary oedema or volume overload.

sections.title: Targets and drugs by condition
items: Malignant hypertension with or without TMA or AKI: labetalol or nicardipine; lower MAP by 20 to 25% over several hours. Hypertensive encephalopathy: lower MAP by 20 to 25% immediately (within the first hour).

Acute ischaemic stroke, not for reperfusion: treat only if BP is above 220/120 mmHg, lowering MAP by about 15% and no more. For thrombolysis or thrombectomy: lower to below 185/110 before and keep below 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after.
Acute intracerebral haemorrhage with SBP above 180 mmHg: lower promptly; ESC advises SBP 130 to 180 mmHg and stroke guidelines commonly target about 140 mmHg. Avoid falls below 130 mmHg.

Acute coronary syndrome: SBP below 140 mmHg immediately with IV nitroglycerin and labetalol (or esmolol). Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema: SBP below 140 mmHg immediately with nitroglycerin or nitroprusside plus a loop diuretic.
Acute aortic dissection: SBP 100 to 120 mmHg and heart rate below 60/min immediately. Beta-blocker (esmolol or labetalol) first, then add nitroprusside, nicardipine or nitroglycerin if needed.
Eclampsia or severe pre-eclampsia or HELLP: BP below 160/105 mmHg immediately with IV labetalol, oral nifedipine (per obstetric protocol) or IV hydralazine, plus magnesium sulphate; plan delivery.
Catecholamine excess (phaeochromocytoma, cocaine, amphetamine): phentolamine; benzodiazepines for stimulant toxicity. Do not give a beta-blocker before alpha blockade.

sections.title: Severe hypertension without organ damage (urgency)
items: Rest in a quiet room, treat pain and anxiety, and recheck BP after 30 minutes; many settle without drugs.
Restart or intensify oral therapy (for example amlodipine, an ACE inhibitor or ARB, or a thiazide-like diuretic) and lower BP gradually over 24 to 48 hours.
Discharge with review within a few days to 1 week; screen for secondary causes and organ damage as an outpatient.

sections.title: Monitoring
items: BP every 5 to 15 minutes during titration (continuous arterial line in ICU), neurological status, ECG, urine output.
Creatinine, potassium and haemoglobin at least daily; watch for AKI from over-rapid lowering.
Nitroprusside: limit high doses and duration, especially with renal or hepatic impairment; watch for cyanide toxicity (metabolic acidosis, rising lactate).

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Treating the number rather than the patient: IV drugs for asymptomatic severe hypertension cause harm.
Aggressive lowering in ischaemic stroke without a reperfusion plan.
Beta-blockers alone in cocaine toxicity or phaeochromocytoma; labetalol in acute heart failure, asthma, bradycardia or heart block.
Missing aortic dissection in a hypertensive patient with chest or back pain and giving thrombolysis or antiplatelets.

drugs.name: Labetalol
drugs.dose: 0.25 to 0.5 mg/kg IV bolus (or 20 mg IV over 2 minutes, then 40 to 80 mg every 10 minutes); infusion 2 to 4 mg/min until target, then 5 to 20 mg/h; maximum cumulative 300 mg
drugs.notes: Avoid in acute HF, asthma, bradycardia, second or third degree AV block.

drugs.name: Nicardipine
drugs.dose: 5 mg/h IV infusion, increase by 2.5 mg/h every 15 to 30 minutes to a maximum of 15 mg/h; reduce to about 3 mg/h once at target
drugs.notes: Avoid in liver failure and severe aortic stenosis. Reflex tachycardia.

drugs.name: Glyceryl trinitrate (nitroglycerin)
drugs.dose: 5 to 200 mcg/min IV infusion, increasing by 5 mcg/min every 5 minutes
drugs.notes: First choice in ACS and pulmonary oedema. Headache; tolerance. Avoid with PDE5 inhibitors.

drugs.name: Sodium nitroprusside
drugs.dose: 0.3 to 10 mcg/kg/min IV infusion, increasing by 0.5 mcg/kg/min every 5 minutes; protect from light
drugs.notes: Arterial line. Cyanide or thiocyanate toxicity with high doses, long infusions, renal or hepatic failure.

drugs.name: Esmolol
drugs.dose: 0.5 to 1 mg/kg IV bolus over 1 minute, then 50 to 300 mcg/kg/min infusion
drugs.notes: Aortic dissection, peri-operative hypertension. Avoid in acute HF and heart block.

drugs.name: Urapidil
drugs.dose: 12.5 to 25 mg IV bolus, then 5 to 40 mg/h infusion

drugs.name: Phentolamine
drugs.dose: 5 mg IV bolus, repeated every 10 minutes as needed to reach the target
drugs.notes: Catecholamine excess (phaeochromocytoma, sympathomimetic toxicity). Tachycardia, angina.
